meta.reviewer: Claude (Opus 5) via Claude Code weekly review
meta.coverage: Top 15 by attention plus sticky accumulate holdovers (TSM, COHR, AMKR, GOOGL). Written 28 August after NVIDIA's Q2 on 26 August and Sivers' Q2 on 27 August, both of which the 25 August pass explicitly predated. GFS and SK Hynix are new here. MU and CCXI drop off the roster. /pre-review was SKIPPED for time, so these verdicts carry no independent seat research this week.
meta.disclaimer: Second-opinion research notes on @aleabitoreddit's ideas. Personal research tool — not investment advice.

focus.headline: Memory repriced. The market sold the news.
focus.dek: Server DRAM up 13–18% next quarter with Samsung asking 20%, MU's 16 LTAs and SNDK's Meta deal lock the demand in — and memory names sold off anyway. SNDK joins the book.

verdicts.view: Upgrade from wait, and the reason is the guide rather than the beat. Q2 revenue was $96.22bn against roughly $92.17bn expected with data centre at $89.0bn, but the number that matters is management guiding fiscal 2028 revenue growth of about 70% on an explicitly supply-constrained outlook, against a 43.9% consensus. Commitments jumped from $119bn to $279bn, largely memory procurement, and hyperscaler capex was framed at roughly $800bn in 2026 rising to $1.3tn in 2027. He is right that the alpha is usually downstream of this print rather than in it, and last week the desk held at wait on the $105bn Portsmouth residual value guaranty, which is unchanged and still under-discussed. But a company adding a 26-point revision to its own multi-year growth rate while the entire supply chain it feeds sells off 20-40% is the cleanest risk-adjusted way to own this week's dislocation.
verdicts.execution: Accumulate on the print rather than chasing the high-beta names. Add in two tranches, the first now and the second only if it retraces to the pre-earnings level around $208-213 seen on 25-27 August. Size at the top tier; this is the position that funds patience elsewhere.
verdicts.changesMind: Any sign the $279bn of commitments is pull-forward rather than demand, a China data centre revenue assumption re-entering guidance, or the Portsmouth guaranty being extended to further counterparties on the same terms.

verdicts.view: Held at wait, and this week is the reason the desk held rather than upgraded. The earnings were genuinely good on the metrics that describe the future: the opportunity pipeline reached $1.2bn, up 268% since December, six new pluggable players appeared with three in alpha sample evaluation, Jabil initial production orders are guided to first half 2027 with the ramp in the second half, and a new foundry partner brings capacity that is available now, which de-risks the single-source dependence on Win Semi. He called it his favourite high-beta optical long and the most unusual $1bn photonics company he has seen. The desk does not dispute any of it. What the desk keeps repeating is the other half: quarterly revenue was $5.64m and adjusted EBITDA was negative $3.72m. The stock fell 33% in a week anyway. That is not the market rejecting the pipeline, it is the market declining to pay a 2027 multiple in a week when it stopped paying for duration at all.
verdicts.execution: No add yet despite the drawdown. This is the highest-beta name in the book and it has now fallen 33% in a week and 13% in a month while the pipeline tripled, which means position sizing rather than conviction is what has been wrong. If already long, hold and do nothing. A first add belongs after the Nasdaq listing removes the Swedish-exchange discount he names himself, or on the first quarter where revenue actually reflects the transition management guides to for Q4 2026.
verdicts.changesMind: The Jabil H1 2027 order date slipping, or the new foundry allocation turning out to be smaller than the language implies. Either one moves this to pass, because pipeline without a dated conversion is the entire bear case.

verdicts.view: Held at wait, and he has now moved most of the way to the desk's position. On 21 August he wrote that it is getting much harder to support the name when they keep dropping $500m and $600m ATMs and that the share structure is becoming shareholder unfriendly. That is the first time this year he has argued against a core holding of his own. He remains long and explicitly overweight versus the rest on the grounds that AOI is genuinely capacity constrained with high demand visibility, and the operating case is intact: Semtech's quarter confirmed TIA and driver shortages, 1.6T FiberEdge qualifications are finishing early, and AOI itself says even combined with Coherent it is very tough to meet customer demand for three years. The stock is down 31% on the week. The desk's read is unchanged from last week: the operating outlook and the per-share outcome have decoupled, and the ATM at $129.10 on the drop from $220 is the reason.
verdicts.execution: No new capital. The demand case does not fix a share count that went from 62.4m to 84.6m in twelve months. Wait for the 1.6T qualification completion to land as revenue rather than as a press line, and for a raise-free quarter, before treating the drawdown as an entry.
verdicts.changesMind: A quarter with no new ATM and 1.6T revenue actually recognised. That combination would move this to accumulate quickly, because the demand side was never the argument.

verdicts.view: Unchanged at accumulate and this is the largest gap in the book between what happened operationally and what happened to the price. It fell 38.5% in a week. Nothing in the evidence moved against it: he reported the fourth consecutive InP substrate price hike with Q4 guided above 10%, described suppliers saying that money alone will not get you material, and Lumentum publicly named AXT as the partner it turned to for additional substrate supply, which is the bottleneck showing up in a customer's own transcript rather than in a channel check. The desk called this the cleanest chokepoint in the book last week and still does. The honest caveat is that filed revenue is $0.09bn and shrinking, so none of the pricing power is in the numbers yet, and in a week when the market stopped paying for 2027 revenue that is exactly the profile that gets sold hardest.
verdicts.execution: This is the one name where the drawdown is an opportunity rather than a warning. Add on weakness in tranches rather than at once, mid-tier size given the $0.1bn revenue base, and accept that the position is volatile by construction. Do not size it like a chokepoint with earnings; it is a chokepoint without them.
verdicts.changesMind: InP substrate pricing rolling over, or a second supplier bringing capacity online faster than expected. The thesis is scarcity; anything that ends scarcity ends the thesis.

verdicts.view: Held at wait on price rather than on the business. The quarter was strong and checks out: $1,006.3m revenue, up 109.3% year on year, 50.4% non-GAAP gross margin, $3.23 non-GAAP EPS and a $1.225-1.275bn guide. He reads the earnings as evidence of extreme demand imbalance in lasers, TIA and DSP with supply years behind demand. The desk agrees and notes the useful detail buried in his own channel-check post: Lumentum and Coherent have too much capacity allocated to NVIDIA to serve the merchant market, which is precisely why the smaller CW names exist as a trade. Down only 7% this week against a 20-40% rout in its smaller peers, which tells you the market is discriminating by size and revenue, not by theme.
verdicts.execution: No add here. Its relative resilience this week is the reason: the dislocation is in the names below it, and paying up for the safest optical name during a rotation out of optical is the wrong end of the trade.
verdicts.changesMind: Gross margin compression as the NVIDIA allocation mix grows, or the merchant CW shortage easing enough to reduce pricing power.

verdicts.view: Unchanged. Down 20% this week on no company-specific news, which is the definition of the rotation rather than a re-rating. The relative-value case the desk made last week is now cheaper: FY2026 non-GAAP gross margin 39.4% and operating margin 20.5% against Lumentum's 46.0% and 29.8%, on materially lower revenue growth, but also on a materially lower multiple. He treats it mostly as a valuation comparator and as the company that confirmed it will not sell indium phosphide lasers externally, which matters more than he lets on: it is the supply decision that creates the merchant gap Sivers and MACOM are trying to fill.
verdicts.execution: Add on this weakness, mid-tier size. This is the liquid, revenue-generating way to hold optical exposure through a drawdown that is punishing the pre-revenue names hardest.
verdicts.changesMind: The internal-only laser policy reversing, which would remove the merchant scarcity that underpins the smaller names and compress the whole complex.

verdicts.view: Downgrade from accumulate, on his evidence rather than the desk's. Two things he wrote this month cut against the position: MACOM's CW capacity does not come online until the second half of 2027, and he judges it likely not meaningfully participating in first-generation CPO deployments, which he frames as a smaller pool of players that Sivers is inside of and MACOM is not. Against that, he also reports the entire optical supply chain out of stock across laser chip, PCB and packaging, and MACOM is one of the suppliers customers are approaching. The desk's problem is timing: a 2027 capacity story with first-generation exclusion, in a week when the market has stopped paying for 2027, does not justify accumulate.
verdicts.execution: Step down to wait rather than sell. No new capital until either the H2 2027 capacity date pulls forward or it appears in a first-generation CPO design win.
verdicts.changesMind: A first-generation CPO participation announcement would reverse this immediately; that is the specific thing he says is missing.

verdicts.view: Held at wait, and the memory case strengthened this week from an unexpected direction. NVIDIA's own commitments rose from $119bn to $279bn largely on memory procurement, and its CFO said the company is experiencing extreme pricing conditions in memory. That is the buyer confirming the shortage the sellers have been claiming. He continues to argue the NAND shortage lasts years because upstream capacity takes up to four years to build, and points to investor-day figures of roughly 80% adjusted gross margin with about $93bn of minimum contracted revenue against a market cap near $239bn. FY2026 GAAP gross margin was already 71.5% against 30.1% a year earlier. The stock still fell 17%. The desk stays at wait only because the entry has been poor all month, not because the case has weakened.
verdicts.execution: No chase. Wait for a retrace toward the pre-selloff level rather than adding into a falling tape; the contracted revenue means the thesis does not expire if you are late.
verdicts.changesMind: Contracted volumes being renegotiated on price, or hyperscaler memory procurement being revealed as double-ordering.

verdicts.view: Unchanged, and this week gave it a date. Sivers guided initial production orders with Jabil in the first half of 2027 and the ramp in the second half, which converts the 1.6T LRO transceiver story from a theme into a scheduled event with a named supplier. He calls Jabil a massive hyperscaler supplier and lists it second among the larger names he likes. The attraction for the desk is unchanged and is now more valuable, not less: at $29.8bn of revenue across healthcare, automotive and connected devices, this is the only way in the book to hold the 1.6T ramp without holding a pre-revenue balance sheet. In a week that punished exactly those balance sheets, that is the point.
verdicts.execution: Add on the 18% weekly drawdown, mid to upper-tier size. This is the defensive expression of the optical thesis and it just went on sale with the rest of the complex.
verdicts.changesMind: The Jabil ramp date slipping alongside Sivers', or EMS margins compressing enough that the optical mix stops mattering to the blended number.

verdicts.view: Initiating at wait. It enters the roster on sustained attention and it sits at a genuine crossroads. He argues the US government taking a material stake plus CPO should re-accelerate revenue, and was surprised the stock was down given a direct government stake advancing CPO, reading it as unrewarded good news. The desk's caution is arithmetic: revenue has been effectively flat near $6.8bn for three years, and the mix is still automotive, IoT and smart mobile rather than AI. The CPO reference design with Sivers is real and is named repeatedly across his posts, but it is a 2027 revenue event attached to a company whose current business is not growing. Down 16% this week.
verdicts.execution: No position yet. Wait for a quarter where specialty photonics revenue is separately visible, or for the CHIPS-linked capacity to convert into a disclosed design-win pipeline.
verdicts.changesMind: Two consecutive quarters of revenue growth attributable to photonics would move this to accumulate; continued flat revenue with CPO still described as future keeps it at wait indefinitely.

verdicts.view: Held at wait. Operationally this remains the most striking set of numbers in the book: Q2 revenue $582.3m, up 454% year on year and 46% sequentially, roughly 50% adjusted EBITDA margin in AI Cloud, $8.04bn of cash, over 5GW contracted and reiterated guidance of $3.0-3.4bn revenue with a $7-9bn exit ARR. This week it was named as the first adopter of Groq3 LPX following NVIDIA's investment, which he reads as the promised early access to latest-generation architectures. It fell 23%. The desk stays at wait because the equity story depends on continuous capital access to build the capacity that is already contracted, and this week demonstrated exactly how fast that access can reprice.
verdicts.execution: No add during the drawdown. The name to watch is the next raise: terms on it will tell you more than another quarter of revenue growth.
verdicts.changesMind: A capital raise on materially worse terms than the last, or contracted power converting to revenue slower than the exit-ARR guide implies.

verdicts.view: Downgrade from wait to pass, and he has argued the desk's case for it twice this month. On 13 August he wrote that it is cash-rich with huge capacity coming but no visible demand to fill it and a weaker moat, and that he holds it only as a deliberate small risk position, explicitly not a clear long. On 21 August he judged that Marvell has probably vertically integrated POET out of the interposer and packaging layer people were speculating about. On 24 August he named it alongside IREN as a company he has criticised for overusing ATMs and dilution, and contrasted it directly against AAOI as the name he is not overweight. Filed revenue rounds to zero across all four years on file. When the analyst who found the name is arguing the bear case, the desk should not be holding a wait.
verdicts.execution: Exit. If there is a position, use any bounce to close it rather than the current level. There is no entry discipline that fixes a story with no revenue, no first-generation participation and a dilution habit.
verdicts.changesMind: A named first-generation CPO design win with disclosed volumes would reopen this; nothing short of that.

verdicts.view: Held at wait, unchanged, and the numbers still argue for more than the price does. Q2 revenue was $11.54bn, up 50%, with gross margin at 53.8% against 39.8% a year earlier, and the company disclosed Data Center revenue of $16.6bn for FY2025, 48% of the total. He argues Helios plus CPUs brings another inflection helped by copying NVIDIA's neocloud fundraise-to-GPU flywheel. Down 7% this week, which is resilient relative to the book. The desk's reservation is the same as last week: roughly 16 times annualised revenue after a large twelve-month move leaves little room for the execution risk in a first Helios cycle.
verdicts.execution: No change. Hold if long; a first add belongs on evidence of Helios design wins rather than on the margin trend, which is already priced.
verdicts.changesMind: A named hyperscaler committing to Helios at volume, or conversely MI-series share loss in the 2027 procurement cycle.

verdicts.view: Unchanged, sticky holdover, and this week the desk corrected its own number rather than his. AI accelerators are not the majority of TSMC; the company does not disclose the share at all, its last hard figure was 6% in 2023, and 2024 AI-related chip sales are estimated near $9.1bn against $88.3bn of revenue. The HPC platform share of roughly 51% is mostly non-AI compute and should not be read as AI exposure. That makes TSMC a slower, cheaper way to own the buildout than the desk had been implying, not a worse one: it fell only 3% this week while its own customers' suppliers fell 20-40%, which is the diversification working. He rarely writes about it directly, so it sits outside the attention ranking on tiering rather than on merit.
verdicts.execution: Continue accumulating on weakness at core size. This is the position that should be largest and least exciting.
verdicts.changesMind: Advanced packaging capacity ceasing to be the constraint, or a leading customer moving meaningful volume to Intel or Samsung foundry.

verdicts.view: Unchanged, sticky holdover. He added personally on weakness he found surprising given the NVIDIA arrangement and a ten-year TSMC agreement, and frames it as more of a 2028 name with separate 2027 ramps. Advanced packaging is the constraint that every accelerator has to pass through, and Amkor is the largest US-headquartered provider of it. The desk's caveat is that communications and automotive packaging still dominate $6.71bn of revenue, so the AI share is real but minority.
verdicts.execution: Hold and add on further weakness at mid-tier size. The 2028 framing is a feature during a week that repriced duration; there is no need to be early.
verdicts.changesMind: TSMC bringing meaningful advanced packaging in-house faster than its own capacity plan implies.

verdicts.view: Initiating at wait. It enters on sustained attention and on this week's confirmation from an unusual direction: NVIDIA's commitments rose to $279bn largely on memory procurement and its CFO described extreme pricing conditions in memory, which is the buyer validating the seller's shortage. He argues US pressure on Apple to avoid Chinese memory hands pricing power back to the non-Chinese suppliers, and that SK Hynix is unveiling a CPO roadmap with a photonic interposer linking to memory, which he reads as TAM expansion for lasers, PICs and packaging. It fell only 1% this week, the best performance in the supply half of the book. The desk holds at wait because the Korean listing is hard to size from a US brokerage and because he expresses this exposure through the EWY basket rather than the line itself.
verdicts.execution: No direct position recommended. If the exposure is wanted, note he holds it via EWY, which is an index basket rather than a company and carries Samsung and the rest of the Korean market with it.
verdicts.changesMind: Chinese DRAM capacity arriving faster than expected, or the CPO-to-memory roadmap slipping out of the 2027-2028 window.

verdicts.view: Unchanged. This week vindicated the framing rather than the position: Amazon rose 1.5% while the suppliers it buys from fell 20-40%. First-half capex of $98.4bn is up 72% and guidance rose to about $220bn explicitly because memory costs went up, which remains the most useful sentence in the quarter for this desk, because Amazon's cost line is Micron's and Sandisk's revenue line. AWS at $42.2bn and up 36.7% is the fastest growth since 2021 with capacity constraints guided to persist into 2027. He keeps routing the trade to Alchip rather than Amazon, which is the right read of where the torque is and, on this week's evidence, the wrong read of risk-adjusted return.
verdicts.execution: Continue accumulating at core size. The week made the case: it is the part of the chain that gets paid regardless of which supplier wins.
verdicts.changesMind: Free cash flow staying negative into a second year without AWS growth accelerating further, which would make the capex a cost rather than an investment.

verdicts.view: Unchanged, sticky holdover, and the same shape as Amazon this week: up 1.1% while the upstream complex was sold. Operating cash flow of $39.07bn against $44.92bn of capital expenditure leaves free cash flow negative, with full-year capex guided to $195-205bn and first-half spend of $80.6bn already close to all of 2025. Cloud growing 82% with record AI demand and backlog justifies it for a balance sheet of this size. He cites the hyperscaler results as proof of the bull case for everything upstream, which is true, and leaves out that the upstream names have no such balance sheet to fund a drawdown with, which this week demonstrated.
verdicts.execution: Continue accumulating at core size, same logic as Amazon.
verdicts.changesMind: A capex pause, which would signal the compute shortage is ending and would hit every name upstream harder than it hits Alphabet.

verdicts.view: Re-entering the roster on score and immediately recorded as pass, which is the same conclusion as 12 August and for the same reason. It ranks twelfth by attention because he name-drops it inside multi-ticker recap posts, not because he argues it: 22 mentions produced 22 views and only three of them are directional. On the humanoid question he is explicit in both directions, writing that Optimus is wrapped inside a trillion-dollar company so it is not the pure-play exposure he is pointing at, and separately that Tesla is targeting general purpose but he does not think they can pull it off yet. Filed revenue is $94.8bn and declining. This is a tiering artefact appearing in a supply-chain book, and the desk should say so rather than write a view it does not hold.
verdicts.execution: No position. It is in the roster because the score put it there, not because there is a case.
verdicts.changesMind: A humanoid programme spun out or separately disclosed, which would make it the pure-play exposure he says it currently is not.
